query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Moderate nickel doping in FeMn-based high-entropy alloys creates a more uniform local spin-exchange environment, enhancing the low-field magnetocaloric effect with minimal hysteresis and preserving mechanical stability by hindering excessive lattice distortion or brittleness.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized FeMn-based high-entropy alloy without nickel addition.
generation.intervention: Systematically replace Fe (or Mn) with Ni in small increments (0–10 at.%) and measure magnetic, thermal, and mechanical properties at each composition.
generation.conditions: Melt and homogenize the alloys; perform magnetocaloric measurements at 0.5–2 T over the cryogenic-to-room temperature range; assess mechanical integrity via standard tensile/impact tests under the same thermal cycling conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized Ni additions alter spin coupling and reduce segregation of magnetic domains, leading to stable ferromagnetic transitions and robust structural cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Nickel substitutions adjust lattice parameters and local electronic structure, narrowing the distribution of exchange energies and shifting the magnetic transition temperature to promote strong, reversible magnetization changes at lower applied fields without large volume changes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Ni-doped samples will exhibit larger isothermal entropy changes and stronger magnetization at low applied fields compared to the baseline, with minimal thermal hysteresis, faster heat exchange cycling, and mechanical properties comparable or superior to the undoped material.
generation.baseline: Undoped FeMn-based high-entropy alloy exhibiting moderate magnetocaloric response but with higher hysteresis and less tunable magnetic transition temperature.
generation.boundary: Applicable up to about 10 at.% Ni substitution. Beyond this limit, excessive lattice distortions could degrade both magnetocaloric performance and mechanical stability.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal doping concentration and processing route remain unclear, and small changes in heat treatment or alloy composition may cause significant deviations in magnetocaloric response or mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce FeMn-based alloys with 0, 2, 5, and 10 at.% Ni, ensuring identical sample dimensions and heat treatments; measure their magnetocaloric effect at 0.5–2 T and across multiple cycles, then compare hysteresis losses, thermal conductivity for heat exchange, and mechanical stress–strain behavior.
measurements: Isothermal magnetization curves and derived magnetic entropy changes
Thermal conductivity for heat exchange rates
Tensile strength and ductility before and after repeated thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Any Ni-doped alloy failing to increase magnetocaloric performance at low fields, showing higher hysteresis, or degrading mechanically compared to the baseline FeMn-based alloy would invalidate the proposed mechanism.

cited_evidence.text: The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. occupying_moves.lever: partial Ni substitution in the FeMn-based high-entropy alloy composition
occupying_moves.technique: arc-melting followed by magnetometric (e.g., VSM), calorimetric, and mechanical testing
occupying_moves.conditions: doping from 0–10 atomic% Ni, low-field (0.5–2 T) cycles, cryogenic-to-room temperatures

chosen.lever: partial Ni substitution in the FeMn-based high-entropy alloy composition
chosen.conditions: 0–10 at.% Ni doping, 0.5–2 T fields, cryogenic-to-room temperature range
chosen.why: We propose a mechanistic hypothesis that moderate Ni doping will tune the local magnetic interactions and microstructure in FeMn-based high-entropy alloys, allowing a strong magnetocaloric response under low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat transfer, minimal hysteresis, and mechanical robustness. The controlled intervention is to vary Ni content (0–10 at.%) and track changes in magnetization, heat exchange, and mechanical stability relative to the undoped baseline. We predict that Ni-doped alloys will exhibit improved low-field magnetocaloric performance, reduced hysteresis, and enhanced mechanical integrity, consistent with prior evidence suggesting that moderate compositional adjustments in high-entropy alloys can fine-tune magnetic phase transitions and mechanical properties. Findings of increased hysteresis or no improvement in magnetocaloric figures of merit under Ni doping would falsify the proposed mechanism.
